wiring.title: Cart wiring, in plain words
steps: Battery (12.8 V LiFePO4) → 30 A fuse → switch → a fuse block with three rails (arm, cart motors, Pi). See the power plan below.

From the block: The cart-motor rail (10 A fuse) goes to the four DRV8871 boards and the TB6612FNG's motor-power pin (the jaws are run at half PWM, about 6 V), the arm rail (10 A fuse, then a 12 V step-down converter) goes to the arm's Waveshare bus servo adapter (it talks to the Pi over USB, so the arm stays on its own USB link and needs no extra wiring), and the Pi rail (3 A fuse) goes to the 12 V → 5 V converter that powers the Pi.

The Pi (a Pi 3 now, a Pi 5 later; the wiring is the same) talks to the PCA9685 over I2C: just 4 wires (3.3 V, ground, SDA, SCL). The PCA9685 then sends two PWM signals to each driver board: one for forward, one for reverse. The jaw TB6612FNG gets its speed from the PCA9685 and its direction from 4 Pi GPIO pins.

Each driver's output goes straight to its motor. Each motor's encoder has 4 wires (power, ground, channel A, channel B): the two channel wires go to Pi GPIO pins, 12 pins in total. If the encoders are 5 V, put the channels through a level shifter first, or power the encoders from the Pi's 3.3 V.
Join all the grounds (battery, drivers, PCA9685, Pi) at one point. Keep thick motor wires away from thin signal wires.
Before the first power-up, with no motors plugged in, check the 5 V and 3.3 V rails with a meter. Then plug in one motor at a time at a low PWM.

items.item: STS3215 servos, 12 V 30 kg version (C018 / Waveshare ST3215 30 kg)
items.note: Follower arm only (no leader). Rule: buy on Amazon UK if servos + board come under about £135; otherwise ArmDojo (Singapore, about S$30 each, free shipping over S$110, ~20% UK VAT on delivery): https://armdojo.com/products/feetech-sts3215-serial-bus-servo. Not stocked by RobotShop UK (twice the price, out of stock), The Pi Hut, Pimoroni, RS or Farnell. Each servo comes with a 15 cm cable. Arrived.

items.item: SO-101 robot arm: 3D-printed parts
items.note: These parts are 3D-printed, not bought: download the STL files and print them in PLA. Design repo: https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100

items.item: Servo driver board (Waveshare Bus Servo Adapter A)
items.note: One board drives all six servos, daisy-chained. No Arduino needed: the laptop runs the software over USB. Also on Amazon UK and ArmDojo (https://armdojo.com/products/waveshare-bus-servo-adapter-board); buy from the same shop as the servos.

items.item: Spare servo cables (3-pin 5264)
items.note: Optional, for longer joint runs. Ready-made connectors.

items.item: USB cable
items.note: Match the driver board's USB-C port.

items.item: 12 V power supply, at least 5 A (100–240 V input)
items.note: Check home first: label must say 12 V and 5 A or more, 5.5 × 2.1 mm barrel plug, centre-positive. Otherwise buy on Amazon. 100–240 V input so it works in Brazil.

items.item: PLA filament, 1 kg spool
items.note: Follower arm needs about 400 g. Weigh the current spool first (subtract about 230 g for an empty plastic spool). Print one test part before the rest.

items.item: Bambu Lab A1 printer (no AMS)
items.note: GTMax3D is an authorised Bambu Lab reseller in Brazil. Other shops: bambulab.com/pt-br/where-to-buy. Pending a chat with Mum.

items.item: PLA/PETG filament
Pipe, tank and plywood
items.note: Bulky and generic, so buy locally.

items.item: Cart drive and hinge motors: 12 V worm-gear motor, 28 mm, with Hall encoder, about 60 rpm
items.for: Cart: 2 pipe drives + 2 hinge worm drives
items.note: Cheapest reliable: the 28 mm 'GA28' / 'JGY-28' style self-locking worm motor with a 2-channel Hall encoder. Pick the 12 V, 50–65 rpm version whose listing shows 3 kg·cm or more rated torque and says 'encoder'. Link is a search because AliExpress listings come and go; check the seller has 500+ sales and 4.7+ stars. Shipping about 2–4 weeks standard (about 10 days with Choice). UK import VAT is added at checkout. Backup if you want it in a week: a similar 12 V worm motor with encoder on eBay UK, about £15 each. Prices are estimates, not quotes. DIMENSIONS: real motors of this type are about 28 mm wide but often 60–75 mm long once the worm box and the encoder cap are counted, against the 55 mm in the CAD; and the worm gearbox puts the output shaft at a right angle to the motor, while the CAD has the motor in line with the worm shaft. Measure the real one and update MOTOR_L and the brackets before cutting anything.

items.item: Jaw motor: N20 worm-gear micro motor with encoder, 6 V, about 30 rpm
items.note: Assumed: the jaw only has to swing 92 degrees against a light grip, so about 0.1–0.2 N·m at the pin is enough; a 6 V N20 worm motor with encoder gives roughly that at 20–40 rpm, and a worm box locks the jaw shut with the power off. Run it at 6 V by capping the PWM at 50% from the 12 V rail. If it turns out too weak, step up to a 12 V N20 at 100 rpm with an extra gear. Shipping 2–4 weeks. DIMENSIONS: an N20 is 12 × 10 mm and about 25 mm long plus gearbox, smaller than the 16 × 30 mm motor + 12 mm box in the CAD (cart_sleeves.py), so it fits, but the right-angle shaft and the keyed pin mount need redrawing. Also check it really has an encoder; many N20 listings sell it as an add-on.

items.item: Motor driver: DRV8871 single H-bridge board (3.6 A peak, 6.5–45 V)
items.note: Swapped in for the TB6612FNG on the four 12 V motors. The TB6612FNG is only rated 1.2 A continuous (3.2 A for a moment) per channel, and a 28 mm worm motor stalled at 12 V can pull 1.5–3 A, so it is under-rated for these. The DRV8871 takes 3.6 A peak, has a current-limit resistor, and needs just two PWM inputs, which the PCA9685 can supply. Also on Amazon UK as 'DRV8871 motor driver' for about £6 each, delivered in 1–2 days: https://www.amazon.co.uk/s?k=DRV8871+motor+driver. Check the real stall current on the motor you receive.

items.item: Motor driver: TB6612FNG dual H-bridge board
items.note: One board runs both jaw motors (about 0.5 A each, well inside its 1.2 A). Pimoroni is the safe UK source (real Pololu-style board, a few pounds more). A generic one from AliExpress is about £2: https://www.aliexpress.com/wholesale?SearchText=TB6612FNG. Only 1 board is needed, not 3, because the big motors use the DRV8871.

items.item: PCA9685 16-channel I2C PWM board
items.note: Gives 16 PWM outputs over two Pi wires (I2C). Six motors need 12 (two per motor), so 4 are spare. A generic board is about £6 on Amazon UK or OnBuy (search 'PCA9685 16 channel'): https://www.amazon.co.uk/s?k=PCA9685+16+channel. Priced here at the cheap one.

items.item: Level shifter, 4-channel 3.3 V / 5 V (bi-directional)
items.note: Needed only if the encoders run on 5 V, as most do: the Pi pins die above 3.3 V. Better: power the encoders from the Pi's 3.3 V pin, which most 5 V Hall encoders accept (check the listing), and skip these. 6 motors × 2 encoder wires = 12 Pi pins; the shifters cover the 5 V case.

items.item: TESTING battery: 12.8 V 7 Ah LiFePO4 (89.6 Wh, under the 100 Wh airline limit)
items.note: Buy this in the UK now so you can test the motors and arm on the bench. Plain words on flying: airlines allow lithium batteries up to 100 Wh in cabin bags without asking. This one is 12.8 V × 7 Ah = 89.6 Wh, so it can go in your hand luggage. It must not go in a checked bag, and the terminals should be covered with tape or the pack kept in a plastic bag. Do NOT buy anything bigger than 100 Wh in the UK. Check the listing says the built-in protection board (BMS) allows 15 A or more continuous; many cheap 7 Ah packs only allow 7–10 A, which is too little when the arm and cart move together. It is not the final battery (see the Brazil one below), and it is too big for the 70 × 50 × 70 mm slot in the CAD, so it sits loose on the bench for now.

items.item: Buck converter 12 V to 5 V, 5 A (for the Pi)
items.note: One 5 A unit covers both the Pi 3 now (needs about 2.5 A, micro-USB) and the Pi 5 later (needs 5 V at up to 5 A over USB-C; the Pi 5 may warn about low current from a simple converter but runs fine). Keep it away from the motor wires.

items.item: Fuse block (6-way blade) + assorted blade fuses (3, 5, 10, 20 A)
items.note: One fuse per rail (see the power plan below): arm 10 A, cart motors 10 A, Pi 3 A (5 A for a Pi 5). The main fuse is the separate 30 A one in the next line.

items.item: Connectors and wire: WAGO lever blocks, JST-XH 4-pin, Dupont jumper wires, 18 AWG and 24 AWG wire
items.note: Thick wire for the 12 V and motor leads, thin for signals. Prices are for one starter kit of each.

items.item: Main fuse: 30 A (MIDI or in-line blade) + holder, and a battery switch
items.note: Fuse right after the battery, then the switch, then the fuse block. Use 12 AWG or thicker (about 3–4 mm²) wire between battery and fuse block; the thin wire in the starter kit is too light for 20 A.

items.item: Heavy wire: 12 AWG (about 4 mm²) red and black, 2 m each, plus ring or spade crimp terminals
items.note: For the battery, fuse, switch and fuse block only.

items.item: FINAL battery: 12.8 V 20 Ah LiFePO4 (256 Wh), BMS 30 A or more
items.note: Buy this in São Paulo so it does not have to fly (256 Wh is over the 100 Wh cabin limit, and airlines would stop it). Price is an estimate from memory of typical Mercado Livre listings (about R$ 700–1,100), not a quote; check it. Look for 'LiFePO4' or 'fosfato de ferro', 12.8 V or 12 V, a BMS rated 30 A, and a listing that shows real size: about 180 × 80 × 170 mm, so it will not fit the 70 × 50 × 70 mm CAD battery slot; the cart design needs a bigger battery space, or the battery rides in the unit and a cable goes to the cart. Alternative if cheap: 4 × 32700 LiFePO4 cells with a 4S 30 A BMS board, about R$ 400, but it needs soldering or spot-welding, so not first choice.

items.item: Solar panel: 100 W monocrystalline, for a 12 V system (peak-power voltage about 18 V)
items.note: A rigid 100 W monocrystalline panel for 12 V batteries, about 1.0 × 0.67 m. Estimate R$ 350–550, not a quote. Also try Minha Casa Solar, Neosolar or Aldo Solar for the same size; a 12 V 'nominal' panel with a maximum-power voltage around 18 V suits the controller below. A flexible panel is lighter but costs more and wears out faster.

items.item: Solar charge controller: MPPT 20 A, 12/24 V, with a LiFePO4 setting
items.note: Must have a lithium / LiFePO4 mode that stops at 14.4–14.6 V; a controller set for lead-acid can overcharge or under-charge the battery. A 100 W panel makes only about 8 A at 12.8 V, so 20 A is plenty with room to grow to 200 W. Estimate R$ 250–600 (Epever is a good brand; cheap no-name PWM controllers at about R$ 80 usually have no LiFePO4 setting, so skip them). Not a quote.

items.item: Solar cable 4 mm² with MC4 connectors (5 m) and a 15 A fuse or breaker between panel and controller
items.note: Estimate, not a quote. Order: panel → fuse → controller → battery. Connect the battery to the controller first, the panel last.

items.item: Step-down converter, adjustable, 10 A, set to 12.0 V (for the arm rail)
items.note: A LiFePO4 battery sits at about 13.3 V full and charges to 14.4 V, but the 12 V arm servos and their adapter are only rated to about 12.6 V. This converter sits between the arm's fuse and the Waveshare adapter and holds it at 12 V. Set it with a meter before connecting the arm. The cart motors can take 13–14 V directly. If a 10 A unit is not available, a 12 V 8 A one is fine: the arm is normally well below that.

power.title: Power for all twelve motors, in plain words
steps: Who draws what, at 12 V. Arm: six STS3215 servos, each about 0.2 A resting, 0.5–1 A moving a load and up to 2.7 A if jammed (stall). Cart: four 28 mm worm motors, about 0.3–0.5 A when running and 1.5–3 A if jammed (assumed, since the listings do not give it), plus two N20 jaw motors, about 0.2 A running, 0.6 A jammed. Pi: a Pi 3 uses about 2–3 W (0.25 A at 12 V), a Pi 5 about 5–12 W (up to 1 A at 12 V). Those figures are from datasheets and typical listings, not measured here.

Typical use (arm moving and one or two cart motors running): about 3–6 A, which is 40–75 W. Idle, with motors holding position and the Pi on: about 0.7–1 A, about 10 W. Worst case you should plan for (three arm servos pushing hard and two cart motors straining at once): about 15–20 A for a moment. Everything stalled at once would be about 30 A, which should never happen and is what the main fuse is for.

Battery: 12.8 V LiFePO4 (4 cells), 20 Ah (256 Wh) for the final robot, with a protection board (BMS) that allows 30 A continuous. For testing in the UK, a 7 Ah (89.6 Wh) pack with a BMS of 15 A or more, which is under the 100 Wh cabin limit. LiFePO4 is safe and gives a steady 12–13 V. One catch: when full it sits at about 13.3 V and charges to 14.4 V, while the STS3215 servos and the Waveshare adapter are only rated to about 12.6 V. So the arm rail goes through a 12 V step-down converter (in the part list). The cart motors can run on the raw battery voltage.

Fuses: 30 A main fuse right after the battery, then a switch, then a fuse block with three rails. (1) Arm rail, 10 A fuse, then the 12 V step-down converter, then the Waveshare adapter; (2) cart motors rail, 10 A fuse, to the four DRV8871 boards and the jaw board; (3) Pi rail, 3 A fuse (5 A for a Pi 5), to the 5 V converter. Splitting them means a jammed arm servo cannot starve the Pi and make it reboot, and a short on the cart motors blows only its own fuse. Join all grounds at one point.

Pi supply: never power the Pi from the motor rail directly; use the 5 V, 5 A converter on its own fuse. On the bench you can instead power the Pi 3 from its normal USB charger (keep a common ground with the rest through the USB-to-adapter cable or one wire).

Daily energy budget (rough): about 2 hours a day of real movement at about 60 W is 120 Wh, plus about 22 hours of waiting at about 5 W (Pi, idle servos, converter losses) is 110 Wh, so about 230 Wh a day, call it 250 Wh. The 256 Wh battery then holds about one day with no sun.

Solar for São Paulo: about 4.5 'full-sun hours' a day on average, about 3.5 in winter (typical published figures, tilted to face north). A panel gives about 70% of its label watts after losses. 250 Wh ÷ (3.5 h × 0.7) is about 100 W, so a 100 W panel just covers the budget in winter and has room to spare in summer. If you move more than 2 hours a day, add a second 100 W panel; the controller already allows it.

What to buy where: battery for testing, fuses, wire, 5 V converter and drivers in the UK now (they are cheap and light). The final battery, solar panel, charge controller and solar cable in Brazil: they are bulky, the battery is too big for the cabin, and Brazilian prices and warranty are easier to deal with locally. Brazil prices here are estimates; check the Mercado Livre pages before paying.
